tests.topic: A pasta factory founded by a grandfather, enlarged by his children and now owned by seven cousins who cannot agree. The saying goes that the first generation builds, the second keeps and the third destroys; the family debates handing the firm to a manager who does not bear its name.

Traditional balsamic vinegar of Modena ages for at least twelve years in a row of ever smaller barrels kept in the attic, where summer heat and winter cold do the work; families once started a set at a daughter's birth. The cheap bottle with a similar name in supermarkets is another product.

A mother and her sixteen-year-old son negotiate Saturday night: he asks for one o'clock because the last bus leaves at half past midnight and his friends stay later, she offers midnight. They settle on conditions: a message when he leaves, and who drives him home.

Maria Montessori opened her first 'Children's House' in 1907 in a poor district of Rome: child-sized furniture, materials chosen freely, a teacher who observes. The passage notes the irony that a method invented for the poorest children is now found mostly in fee-paying schools.

An engineer keeps her job with a Milan company while living again in her home town in Puglia: lower rent, the sea and her parents nearby, against a slow connection, no colleagues to talk to, and the suspicion that those who stay in the office are promoted first.

A family doctor describes patients who leave disappointed when she refuses antibiotics for flu, which is caused by a virus the drugs cannot touch. She explains how every needless course helps bacteria learn to resist, and why a country fond of these medicines pays the price in its hospitals.

The night train from Milan to Sicily does something rare in Europe: at the Strait of Messina the carriages are uncoupled and pushed into the hull of a ferry, with the passengers still on board. The journey takes some twenty hours, and the passage asks who still chooses it over a flight.

Roman harbour walls have stood in sea water for two thousand years, while modern concrete can crack within decades. The Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash, and researchers have found that small lumps of lime in the mix let cracks seal themselves when water enters.

A daughter challenges her father's habit of carrying six-packs of bottled mineral water up the stairs every week when the tap water is tested and safe. He talks of taste and limescale, she of plastic and cost; they agree on a blind tasting to settle it.

From 1927 the Mille Miglia sent racing cars at full speed over a thousand miles of ordinary roads, from Brescia to Rome and back, through villages lined with spectators. A crash that killed onlookers ended it in 1957; it survives as a parade of historic cars where precision counts, not speed.

In the 1950s the novelist Italo Calvino gathered two hundred folk tales from every Italian region into one book, as the Grimm brothers had done for Germany. He chose among versions, joined pieces and admitted adding touches of his own: the old proverb says a tale is nothing unless you add to it.

In 1965 the typewriter maker Olivetti presented a programmable calculator small enough to stand on a desk, at a time when computers filled rooms; it sold tens of thousands, some to the American space agency. The passage asks why the company did not go on to lead the industry it had anticipated.

In February 1951 a Florentine businessman invited a handful of American buyers to his home to see dresses by Italian designers, days after the Paris shows. The clothes were simpler, easier to wear and cheaper than French couture, and the evening is counted as the birth of Italian fashion.

Giuseppe Verdi used his fortune to build in Milan a rest home for musicians who had grown old without money, and called it his finest work. It still operates: retired singers and players live there alongside conservatory students, and the passage describes what each group gives the other.

In a museum of modern art two friends stop before a canvas of one colour with a single cut in it. 'I could do that,' says one; the other, who has read the label, explains what the artist wanted to open beyond the surface, and asks why nobody had done it before him.

In the 1960s state television broadcast, in the early evening, lessons for adults who could not read or write. A schoolteacher drew with charcoal on large sheets and never made a pupil feel ashamed; groups followed in bars and parish halls, and well over a million people gained their primary certificate.

On a high plain in Abruzzo saffron is harvested for two weeks in autumn: the purple flowers are picked by hand at dawn before they open, and the three red threads of each are pulled out the same day at the kitchen table. Some two hundred thousand flowers make one kilo, which explains the price.

The tobacconist's, marked by a sign with a large T, sells under state licence far more than cigarettes: stamps, bus tickets, lottery slips, phone credit, and a counter where bills and fines are paid. The passage explains how a shop for a declining product became a small public office.

A granddaughter tries to write down her grandmother's ragù: she asks for grams and minutes, the grandmother answers 'as much as it needs' and 'until it looks right'. Their exchange shows the gap between cooking by eye and cooking from a recipe, and they end with a compromise.

A Calabrian family meets for the first time the descendants of a great-uncle who emigrated to Argentina a century ago: the same surname, the grandmother's recipes changed by different ingredients, old photographs compared at the table, and the odd feeling of being relatives and strangers.

In the 1950s a priest sent to a handful of farmhouses in the Tuscan hills opened a school for boys the state school had failed: lessons all day, every day of the year, the older teaching the younger, newspapers as textbooks. With his pupils he wrote a letter accusing schools of losing the poor.

A university student delivers meals by bicycle: he is paid per delivery, an app decides who gets the orders, and rainy evenings pay best. He calls it freedom because he chooses his hours; the passage sets that against no sick pay and a broken bicycle that is his own problem.

For generations Italian doctors have prescribed a fortnight at a spa town: hot mud for the joints, sulphur water to breathe, partly paid for by the health service. The passage traces the habit back to Roman baths and weighs thin scientific evidence against patients who return every year.

Some of the trams running in Milan today were built around 1928: wooden benches, brass handles, a bell worked by the driver's foot. The city keeps them because they are simple to repair and people love them, though they have steps a wheelchair cannot climb.

A couple compare two flats after a day of viewings: one in the historic centre, third floor without a lift, thick walls and painted beams, where even the window frames cannot be changed without permission; one in a new block on the edge of town with a garage and a balcony.

In a summer of drought the Po shrinks until sandbanks and old wrecks appear, and something less visible happens at its mouth: sea water pushes many kilometres up the river bed. Farmers of the delta who pump river water onto their fields find it salty, and the rice suffers first.

Many of the 'iron paths' of the Dolomites, routes fitted with steel cables and ladders, were first laid by soldiers during the First World War to move troops across rock faces. Today hikers clip onto them for pleasure; the passage describes one route and the tunnels and trenches still beside it.

Primo Levi worked all his life as a chemist in a paint factory and wrote in the evenings. He said the laboratory taught him to weigh words as precisely as substances; his first book, about his deportation, was turned down by a major publisher and read widely only ten years later.

In the 1930s a group of physicists in their twenties worked under Enrico Fermi in a Roman institute in via Panisperna. One morning in 1934 they found that neutrons passed through paraffin or water became far more effective, a result tested, it is said, in the garden's goldfish pond. Within a few years the group had scattered.

Beside motorway exits stand outlet centres built like small towns, with a square, a bell tower and fountains, where designer clothes of past seasons sell at a discount. The passage looks at who really saves, at goods made specially for outlets, and at the old shopping streets left emptier.

After eight years of piano at the conservatory, with two to go before the diploma, a seventeen-year-old tells her mother she wants to stop and make electronic music on a computer. The mother speaks of wasted years and a certificate; the daughter of what she actually listens to and writes.

In 1962 two designer brothers wanted a light above the dining table without drilling the ceiling. Their answer was a steel arch rising from a block of marble weighing over sixty kilos, with a hole through it so that two people can lift it on a broom handle. Every detail answers a practical problem.

On an October night in 1963 a whole mountainside slid into the reservoir behind one of the world's tallest dams, in the north-east. The dam held; the wave that passed over it wiped out the town below. For years engineers and a local journalist had warned that the slope was moving.

Some farmers have gone back to wheat varieties grown a century ago: taller plants that the wind flattens, half the harvest per hectare, flour sold at three times the price. The passage sets out the growers' reasons (taste, hardiness, a market) and the doubt that it is partly fashion.

A young mechanic asks a bank officer for a loan to open a bicycle repair shop. She questions him on rent, expected customers and what happens in winter; he has figures for some answers and not for others, and learns why the bank wants his parents' signature as a guarantee.

The aperitivo began as a glass of vermouth before dinner in Turin; in Milan it grew into a buffet included in the price of a drink, which students use as a cheap dinner. The passage sets out who gains (bars, young customers) and who complains (restaurants, nutritionists).

A girl with no brothers, sisters or cousins compares her Sunday lunch of five people with her grandfather's memories of twenty at one table. With so few children born, the passage weighs what an only child gains (attention, resources) and what quietly disappears.

The life of a student from the South at university in Bologna: a shared flat, a rent that eats most of the budget, the long train home and the return with a suitcase of food from his mother. Who can afford to study away from home, and who cannot.

A public competitive exam: several thousand candidates fill a sports hall to compete for a few dozen permanent posts in a town administration. The passage follows one candidate through the day and explains why the 'permanent job' still attracts in a market of short contracts.

In 1978 Italy passed a law to close its psychiatric hospitals, inspired by a doctor in Trieste who had opened the gates, removed the restraints and let patients walk into town. The passage tells what replaced the asylums, and what burden passed to families where local services were never built.

By 1990 the tower of Pisa leaned so far that it was closed for fear of collapse. Engineers did not push it: they slowly removed soil from under the higher side until it settled back by about forty-five centimetres. They deliberately stopped there, because a straight tower would no longer be the tower of Pisa.

Two friends plan a week in Sardinia in July and compare ways of getting there: the overnight ferry with their own car and a night on deck, or a one-hour flight and a hired car. They count money, hours and luggage, and each ends up defending the option the other first proposed.

A nearly abandoned mountain village in Abruzzo is restored as a 'scattered hotel': rooms spread among the old houses, smoke-blackened walls left as they were, jobs for the few remaining residents. Critics ask whether the village has been saved or turned into a stage set for visitors.

Italy has more forest today than a century ago, because hill farms were abandoned and trees took back the fields. Good news for deer and boar; yet untended terraces collapse, paths vanish and dense young woods burn easily, so 'more trees' is not simply better.

At the London Olympics of 1908 the baker's boy Dorando Pietri entered the stadium first in the marathon, exhausted, turned the wrong way and fell several times; officials helped him over the line and he was disqualified for it. The loser became far more famous than the winner.

Italy's best-known literary prize began in 1947 in a Roman drawing room where writers and friends met on Sundays, and took its name from the liqueur made by the family that paid for it. Several hundred 'friends' still vote; the passage asks what a winning band on the cover does for a book.

Antonio Meucci, a Florentine emigrant in New York, built a device to speak from his workshop to the room where his sick wife lay. Too poor to keep paying the ten dollars that protected his idea, he let it lapse; Bell patented the telephone in 1876. Who counts as the inventor of something?

On a seaside promenade a girl is tempted by a copy of a designer bag at a twentieth of the price. Her friend objects: the buyer too can be fined, nobody knows who sewed it and in what conditions, and the stitching will not last the summer. The first replies that the real one is priced for the name.

The commedia dell'arte of the sixteenth century: travelling companies of paid actors, each specialised for life in one masked character, who improvised around a plot pinned up backstage instead of a written script. It was also the first theatre in which women played the women's parts.

Caravaggio painted saints and madonnas using people from the Roman streets as models: wrinkled faces, torn clothes, the dirty soles of a pilgrim's feet in the foreground. Some churches refused the paintings as indecent, collectors bought them at once, and the passage explains what was new in his light.

Between the late 1950s and early 1960s Italy changed from a farming country into an industrial one: a refrigerator, a television and a small Fiat entered ordinary homes, bought in instalments. The passage follows one family across those years and counts what the 'economic miracle' cost as well as gave.

A bacterium carried by a tiny insect has dried out millions of olive trees in southern Puglia, some of them centuries old. Farmers at first resisted orders to cut down infected trees they had inherited; the passage explains the reasons on both sides and the replanting with resistant varieties.

How a consumer cooperative supermarket differs from an ordinary chain: born among workers in nineteenth-century Turin to buy food at fair prices, it is owned by its members, each with one vote however much they spend. The passage asks how much of that idea a shopper still notices today.

The Slow Food movement, born in Piedmont in the 1980s after a fast-food restaurant opened beside a famous Roman square: its idea of food that is 'good, clean and fair', its defence of small producers, and the objection that such food costs more than many families can spend.

Three siblings inherit their grandparents' house in a hill village: one wants to sell, one wants it for the summers, one lives abroad and does not answer. The house stays shut for years, costing taxes and repairs, a common fate of inherited homes in emptying villages.

The school-leaving exam (maturità): the ritual night before, the written papers, the oral in front of a board of teachers, and the curious fact that many adults still dream decades later of sitting it unprepared. Why one exam weighs so much in memory.

A young biologist who moved to a Dutch university compares the two lives: there a salary, a contract and equipment; here her family, her friends and Sunday lunch. She explains why she left, what would make her return, and why she dislikes being called a 'brain on the run'.

In an emergency department a boy with a sprained ankle complains that people who arrived after him are seen first. The triage nurse explains the colour codes: patients are ordered by danger, not by arrival, and a long wait is in a sense good news.

A nurse travels fifty minutes each way on a regional train, often standing, on a line where a delay of twenty minutes is ordinary. She sets her journey beside the fast, comfortable trains between big cities and asks why a railway seems to run at two speeds for two kinds of passenger.

An old Italian town is built around its square: church, town hall, market and café face one another, and people cross it many times a day. Districts built since the 1960s often have car parks instead, and the passage asks whether a shopping centre can do the same job.

Why the Po Valley has some of the most polluted air in Europe in winter: the plain is closed on three sides by mountains, wind is rare, and a lid of cold air traps the smoke of traffic, heating and farms. Traffic bans on single days change little, and the passage explains why.

Each June four districts of Florence play a game in Renaissance costume on a square covered with sand: twenty-seven players a side, fifty minutes, the ball carried by any means, and wrestling allowed. Admirers see living history, critics see a licensed brawl, and the rules have been tightened more than once.

Dante was banished from Florence in 1302 and never saw it again; he wrote his great poem moving between the courts of other cities, placing his enemies in hell. He died in Ravenna, which has refused ever since to give his bones back to Florence.

For the school newspaper a student interviews a volcanologist who watches Vesuvius: which signals the instruments record day and night, how many days' warning he would expect, what the evacuation plan asks of the hundreds of thousands living in the danger zone, and why people go on living there.

A Neapolitan tailor's jacket takes some thirty hours of hand sewing and three fittings: a soft shoulder with no padding, sleeves set like a shirt's. Few local boys will train for years before earning, and the tailor's newest apprentices have come from Japan and Korea to learn.

The singer-songwriter Fabrizio De André wrote in the 1960s and 70s about thieves, prostitutes and the defeated, and was watched with suspicion. Today his lyrics appear in school anthologies beside the poets; the passage asks what changes when a song of protest becomes homework.

Since 1969 a special unit of the Carabinieri has traced stolen paintings and objects dug illegally from ancient tombs, using a huge database of photographs. The passage follows the recovery of one vase from grave robbers to a foreign museum and back, and why an object without its site loses its story.

Centuries before modern factories, the shipyard of Venice built galleys from standard parts stored in order along a canal: the hull was towed past warehouses and received masts, oars and weapons in turn. For a visiting French king in 1574, a ship was reportedly fitted out during a banquet.

On the steepest slopes of the Alps and the Ligurian coast grapes are still grown on narrow terraces where no tractor can go: everything is carried on the back or on a small monorail. A bottle costs several times more to produce, and the passage asks why growers continue.

A Tuscan leather workshop that sews bags for famous brands under contract: the craft is the workshop's, the name on the bag and most of the price belong to someone else. The owner weighs the safety of steady orders against the risk of launching a brand of his own.

Why Italy has hundreds of pasta shapes and cooks insist each belongs with certain sauces: ridges, holes and rough surfaces hold sauce differently, and pasta pushed through bronze dies is rougher than the smooth industrial kind. A matter of physics as much as habit.

A 28-year-old with a short-term contract still lives in his childhood bedroom, like many Italians of his age. He lists the reasons (rents, unstable pay), the comforts (meals, laundry) and the embarrassments, and rejects the label of 'big baby' that newspapers give his generation.

Fewer pupils each year choose the liceo classico, with its five years of Latin and ancient Greek. Critics call it a school of the past; an engineer who attended one argues that translating a difficult page trained her to solve problems. The passage sets out both cases.

Before his interview for a summer job as a waiter in a seaside town, a seventeen-year-old asks his older cousin for advice: insist on a written contract, ask about hours and the day off, find out how tips are shared, and do not accept 'a trial week' without pay.

Mountain villages in eastern Sardinia have an unusual number of people over a hundred, many of them men. Researchers point to steep daily walks, simple food, close families and inherited traits, and the passage warns against selling any single one of these as the secret.

In a city without roads everything moves by boat and handcart: parcels, building materials, rubbish, ambulances, even removals. The passage follows a delivery man over bridges with steps and explains why the same goods cost more in Venice and must arrive early in the morning.

After an earthquake destroyed a town in Friuli in 1976, its people chose to rebuild 'where it was, as it was', numbering the stones of the cathedral to put them back. The passage contrasts this with towns moved to new sites after other earthquakes, which residents never felt were theirs.

A blue crab from the Atlantic coast of America, probably carried in the ballast water of ships, has multiplied in the lagoons of the northern Adriatic, where it cuts nets and eats the clams that fishermen farm. Some now sell the crab itself; the passage asks whether eating an invader can stop it.

In the years after the war two cyclists divided Italy: Bartali, older, devout and stubborn, and Coppi, modern and fragile. A famous photograph shows a bottle passing between them on a climb, and people still argue about who was handing it to whom. What a sporting rivalry gave a poor country.

Two classmates disagree about the nineteenth-century novel every Italian pupil must read: one found it endless, the other was gripped by the chapters on the plague in Milan. They ask whether making a classic compulsory creates readers or puts them off for life.

Physics laboratories lie beside a motorway tunnel under the Gran Sasso, beneath 1,400 metres of rock. The mountain screens out the rain of particles from space so that instruments can catch extremely rare signals; the passage explains why some experiments need 'silence' rather than power.

For more than a century the Tuscan town of Prato has turned old woollen clothes into new cloth: workers sort rags by colour and quality by hand, the fibres are shredded and spun again without new dye. A trade once thought poor now looks ahead of its time.

The most famous Neapolitan song was composed in 1898 far from the sun it praises, by a musician on tour in a cold city on the Black Sea. He and the poet sold it to a publisher for a few lire, it travelled the world, and both men died poor.

Michelangelo carved his David from a tall, narrow block of marble that other sculptors had abandoned as flawed and that had lain in a yard for decades. Moving the finished statue to the square took four days; since the nineteenth century a copy stands there, and the passage asks whether visitors mind.

A medieval Florentine merchant going to a fair in Flanders did not carry gold over roads full of robbers: he paid in at a bank at home and travelled with a letter to be cashed at the bank's branch abroad. The passage explains the trick and how it made the bankers richer than princes.

The Etruscans built their cities largely of wood and clay, which vanished, and their tombs of stone, furnished like houses, which remain. So almost everything known about their life comes from their dead: painted banquets where wives recline beside husbands, a custom that scandalised Greek writers.

A daughter studying agriculture wants to convert her family's farm to organic methods; her father doubts it: lower yields, three years before the label can be used, more paperwork. She answers with prices and the health of the soil, and they agree to try on one field first.

A market trader who sets up his cheese stall in five different towns each week: the licence for each pitch, the start at five in the morning, and why, in his view, online shopping has taken customers from shops but not from him.

In 1891 Pellegrino Artusi, a retired silk merchant, published at his own expense a book of recipes that no publisher wanted. Housewives from all over the country wrote to him with dishes of their own, each edition grew, and a book made by post gave kitchens of different regions a shared table.

A grandmother collects two grandchildren from school every day because nursery places are few and both parents work. She is proud and tired in equal measure, and the family is thrown into confusion the day she announces she wants Thursdays for herself.

Two classmates discuss whether one of them should spend the fourth year of high school in Ireland: what she would gain, the subjects she would have to make up on her return, the cost to her parents, and her fear that the class will have moved on without her.

One of the last shipwrights who build wooden fishing boats by hand in a Ligurian harbour: he chooses the timber himself, works without drawings, and has no apprentice because the training is long and fibreglass boats are cheaper. What disappears when a trade is not handed on.

Just after her eighteenth birthday a girl goes with her father to give blood for the first time: the questionnaire, the ten minutes on the couch, the breakfast offered afterwards. The passage explains why donation in Italy is unpaid on principle, and why that is thought to make blood safer.

The Autostrada del Sole, built between 1956 and 1964, joined Milan to Naples and cut a journey of two days to under eight hours. It brought families, goods and holidays closer together; it also tied the country to cars and lorries rather than railways.

The villas Palladio designed for Venetian landowners in the sixteenth century look like temples, with columns and a triangular front, yet they were working farms: the wings held barns, stables and stores. The passage explains the logic of the design and why it was copied as far away as America.

In July 1976 a chemical plant north of Milan released a cloud containing a poison over the town of Seveso. Residents were told days later; animals died, children's skin was marked, a district was evacuated and buried under what is now a wooded park. European rules on industrial risk bear the town's name.

A fourteen-year-old tells her father she wants to leave volleyball for the girls' football team that has started in town. He hesitates about injuries and what people will say; she replies with her brother's example, and he recalls that in his day no such team existed for his sister.

In 1962 two sisters in Milan launched a comic about a masked thief, printed in a small format so that commuters could read it on the train and slip it in a pocket. A criminal as hero caused scandal and court cases; the series is still on sale at newsstands.

Barred from the university by the racial laws of 1938, the young doctor Rita Levi-Montalcini set up a laboratory in her bedroom, studying chick embryos with sewing needles as instruments while the war went on. The work begun there led to a Nobel Prize in 1986.

A hat factory founded in Alessandria in the nineteenth century still makes felt hats in some fifty steps over seven weeks, on machines a century old. When men stopped wearing hats in the 1960s the town lost thousands of jobs; cinema and a few loyal customers kept the name alive.

For the Italian westerns of the 1960s the composer Ennio Morricone had too little money for a full orchestra, so he wrote for a whistler, a whip, a bell, an electric guitar and a voice without words. The limitation produced a sound that people recognise within three notes.

When the Arno flooded Florence in November 1966, mud and heating oil covered books and paintings. Thousands of young volunteers from Italy and abroad, later called the 'mud angels', carried them out by hand, and the emergency forced restorers to invent methods still in use.

A girl records her grandfather for a school project: in 1961 he left a village in Puglia for the car factories of Turin, with a cardboard suitcase and one address. He recalls signs refusing to rent to southerners, the fog, the first pay packet, and why he never went back to live.

In the plains of Campania mozzarella is made from the milk of water buffalo, richer in fat than cow's milk, and is at its best within hours. The passage follows a dairy from the dawn milking to the hand-shaping of the curd, and explains why locals say the cheese should never see a refrigerator.
